terms.definition: The speed at which the drill bit deepens the borehole, typically measured in feet per hour (ft/hr) or meters per hour (m/hr).
The amount of downward force exerted on the drill bit by the drill collars/drill string to crush and cut rock formations.
Rotational speed of the drill string or mud motor powering the drill bit.
Total pressure required to circulate drilling fluid down through the drill string and up the annulus.
High-pressure safety valve assembly installed at the wellhead to seal the wellbore and prevent uncontrolled fluid escape (blowout).
Solid materials (nutshells, mica, fibers, calcium carbonate) added to drilling mud to seal fractures or cavernous formations causing mud loss.
The effective density exerted by circulating mud against formation walls, including hydrostatic pressure plus annular friction pressure drop.
Unscheduled rig downtime caused by equipment failures, stuck pipe, weather delays, or wellbore instability issues.
An unplanned flow of formation fluids (gas, oil, or water) entering the wellbore when formation pore pressure exceeds hydrostatic pressure.
A condition where the drill string cannot be pulled, rotated, or lowered due to differential pressure sticking, key seating, or hole collapse.
The vertical distance from a surface reference point (e.g. RKB) to a point in the wellbore trajectory.
The total length of the wellbore path as measured along the actual drilled hole.
A measure of the curvature or total change in inclination and azimuth along a normalized course length (typically 100 ft or 30 m).
The lower portion of the drill string consisting of the bit, bit sub, mud motor/RSS, MWD/LWD tools, stabilizers, and drill collars.
Real-time downhole sensor package transmitting directional surveys (inclination, azimuth, toolface) to surface via mud pulse telemetry.
Formation evaluation sensors (gamma ray, resistivity, density, neutron porosity) integrated into the BHA for real-time petrophysical data.
A pressure test performed just below a newly set casing shoe to determine fracture gradient and maximum allowable mud weight.
A limit pressure test to verify the casing shoe and formation can withstand a specified maximum planned mud weight without fracturing.
The uppermost depth level reached by cured cement in the casing-borehole annulus.
The density of the drilling fluid used to provide hydrostatic balance against formation pore fluid pressure and stabilize borehole walls.
The slope of the shear stress versus shear rate curve above yield point, representing mechanical friction between mud solids and liquids.
The initial resistance of drilling fluid to flow, representing electrochemical attractive forces among particles in the fluid under dynamic conditions.
A cutting element composed of a diamond table bonded to a tungsten carbide substrate, widely used on modern fixed-cutter rotary bits.
The measured depth at which a vertical wellbore is deliberately deflected into a directional trajectory.
The length of casing between the guide shoe and the float collar, holding contaminated tail cement to prevent weak cement at shoe.
The upward speed of drilling mud traveling through the space between the drill string and the borehole wall or casing.
Sticking of the drill string against a permeable formation caused by the overbalance pressure of the mud column holding the pipe into filter cake.
terms.typical_units: psi overbalance, contact area sq in

terms.definition: Accumulation of drill cuttings or cavings around the drill string that chokes the annulus, causing sudden standpipe pressure spikes and lost returns.
Mechanical parting or catastrophic shear failure of the drill string due to excessive torque, fatigue, or cyclic stress.
A highly toxic, flammable, and corrosive gas (sour gas) encountered in certain carbonate and clastic hydrocarbon formations.
